translations.text: Jesus took his twelve disciples: and the rest.
Here it is read in this gospel, which we have just heard from the deacon's mouth, that "the Saviour took his twelve disciples aside,
and said to them, Behold, we must go to the city of Jerusalem, and then all the things that were written about me by the prophets will be fulfilled.
"I shall be betrayed to the nations, and they will treat me with scorn, and scourge me, and afterwards kill me, and I will rise from death on the third day."
Then his disciples had no understanding of these words. Then it happened that they drew near to a city called Jericho, and a certain blind man was sitting there by the road;
and when he heard the people going along with the Saviour, he asked who was passing there.
They told him that it was the Saviour passing. Then he began to cry out, and said, "Saviour, Son of David, have mercy on me."
The people who were going ahead of the Saviour rebuked the blind man, telling him to be silent.
Then he cried out much more loudly, "Saviour, Son of David, have mercy on me." Then the Saviour stood still and ordered the blind man to be led to him.
When he drew near, the Saviour asked him, What do you want me to do for you?
He said, Lord, that I may see. And the Saviour said to him, Look now: your faith has healed you.
And he at once saw, and followed the Saviour, and glorified him. Then all the people who saw that miracle praised God with great fervour."
The beginning of this gospel touched on our Saviour's passion, yet he did not suffer at this time;
but he wished to make known his passion to his disciples far and long beforehand, so that they would not be too greatly frightened by the passion when the time came that he would suffer.
Their minds were frightened by Christ's words, but he encouraged them again with what he said:
"I will rise from death on the third day." Then he wanted to strengthen and confirm their faith with miracles.
And they then came to the place where the blind man sat by the road, and Christ healed him in the sight of the whole company, because he wished to bring them to faith by that miracle.
However, the miracles that Christ worked showed one thing through power, and signified another thing through mystery.

He truly worked those miracles through divine power, and with those miracles he confirmed the people's faith; but yet there was another thing hidden in those miracles, according to the spiritual sense.
This one blind man signified all mankind, which was blinded through Adam's sin, and thrust out of the joy of paradise, and brought into this life, which is compared to a prison.
Now we are locked out from the heavenly light, and in this life we cannot enjoy the eternal light; nor do we know any more of it than as much as we read in books through Christ's teaching.
This world, though it may sometimes seem pleasant, is nevertheless no more like the eternal world than a prison is like bright daylight.
All mankind was, as we said before, blinded with unbelief and error; but through Christ's coming we were drawn out of our errors and enlightened through faith.
Now we have the light in our minds, which is faith in Christ; and we have the hope of the joy of eternal life, though we still dwell bodily in our prison.
The blind man sat at the city called Jericho. Jericho is interpreted as, and means, 'moon.' The moon both waxes and wanes: for half the month it is waxing, for half it is waning.
Now the moon signifies our mortal life and the decay of our mortality. At one end people are born; at the other end they pass away.
When Christ came to the city of Jericho, which signifies the moon, then the blind man received sight.
That is, when Christ came to our mortality and took on our human nature, then mankind was enlightened and received sight.
He sat by the way; and Christ said in his gospel, "I am the way, and the truth, and the life."
The man who knows nothing of the eternal light is blind; but if he believes in the Saviour, then he sits by the way.

If he will not ask for the eternal light, then he sits blind by the way without asking. He who rightly believes in Christ, and earnestly prays for the enlightenment of his soul, sits by the way asking.
Whoever recognizes the blindness of his mind, let him cry out with inward heart, just as the blind man cried out, "Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me."
The crowd that went before Jesus rebuked the blind man, and told him to be quiet.
The crowd signifies our evil desires and sins, which cry out at us and oppress our hearts, so that we cannot pray as earnestly as we ought.
It often happens, when a man wants to turn away from evil, and atone for his sins, and turn to God with all his mind, that the old sins which he committed before come
and trouble his mind, and want to silence his voice, so that he does not call out to God. But what did the blind man do when the people wanted to silence him?
He cried out all the more, until Jesus heard his voice and healed him. So we also must do, if the devil torments us with manifold thoughts and temptations:
we must cry out more and more to Jesus, that he drive away the evil temptations from our heart, and that he enlighten our mind with his grace.

If, then, we persevere in our prayers, we can bring it about with our crying out that the Saviour, who was walking on before, stands still and will hear our calling, and enlighten our hearts with good and pure thoughts.
Evil thoughts cannot harm us, if they do not please us;
but the more the devil terrifies us with evil thoughts, the better we are, and the dearer to God, if we despise the devil and all his temptations, through God's help.
What is Jesus' standing, or what is his passing? He passed by through his human nature, and he stood through his divine nature.
He passed through his human nature, in that he was born, and went from place to place, and suffered death, and arose from death, and ascended to heaven. This is his passing.
He stands through his divine nature; because he is present everywhere through his might, and has no need to go from place to place; because he is in every place through his divinity.
When he passed by, he heard the blind man's crying; and when he stood, he gave him sight;
for through his human nature he pities the blindness of our mind, and through his divine nature he grants us light and enlightens our blindness.
He said to the blind man, "What do you want me to do for you?" Do you think that he who was able to heal him did not know what the blind man wanted?
But he wanted the blind man to ask, because he urges everyone very insistently to pray. Yet he says in another place,
"Your heavenly Father knows what you need before you ask him for anything." Even so, the good God wants us to pray to him earnestly, because through prayer our heart is stirred and turned to God.
Then the blind man said, "O lord, grant that I may see." The blind man asked neither for gold, nor silver, nor any worldly thing, but asked for his sight.
He reckoned it worthless to ask for anything but sight; for though the blind man may have something, he cannot see without light what he has.
Let us therefore imitate this man, who was healed by Christ both in body and in soul: let us not ask for false riches, nor for transitory honours;
but let us ask our Lord for light: not the light that comes to an end, that is driven away by the night, that is common to us and to beasts;
but let us ask for the light which we can see only with the angels, which will never be ended.
To that light truly our faith must bring us, just as Christ said to the blind man, "Look now, your faith has healed you."
Now some unbelieving man will ask, "How can I desire the spiritual light, which I cannot see?"
Now I say to that man that the things he understands and can perceive, he does not perceive through his body but through his soul; and yet no one sees his soul in this life.
It is invisible, yet it guides the visible body. The body, which is visible, has life from the soul, which is invisible.
Let the invisible depart, and the visible falls down, because it never stood by itself. The life of the body is the soul, and the life of the soul is God.
If the soul departs, the mouth cannot speak, though it gapes; nor can the eye see, though it is open; nor does any limb do anything, if the body is without a soul.
So too the soul: if God forsakes it because of sins, it does nothing good.
No one can do anything good without God's help. Yet the sinful soul is not turned to nothing altogether, though it is dead to God;
but it is dead to every virtue and happiness, and is kept for the eternal death, where it remains forever in torments, and yet never perishes.
How can you now doubt the eternal light, though it is invisible, when you have life from an invisible soul, and you do not doubt at all that you have a soul, though you cannot see it?
When the blind man could see, he followed the Saviour. The man who can understand God and does good works sees and follows God.
The man who understands God and will not do good sees but will not follow God. But let us understand God and do good works: let us watch where Christ goes, and follow him;
That is, we must consider what he teaches and what pleases him, and carry it out in our deeds, just as he himself said:
"Whoever serves me, let him follow me"; that is, let him imitate me, shun every evil and love every good, as I do. Christ did not take land or wealth for himself in this life, as he said of himself:
"Wild animals have holes, and birds have nests where they rest, but I have nowhere to lay my head."
He who owns all things had only as much as he cared to have, and lived on other men's possessions.
We read in Christ's book that the people plotted about him, that they wanted to seize him and raise him up as king, so that he would be their head in worldly matters, as he was in divine ones.
When Christ perceived the people's will, he fled alone to a mountain, and his companions went to the sea, and the Saviour was up on land.
Then at night the Saviour went over the water with dry feet until he came to his disciples, where they were rowing.
He fled worldly honour when he was chosen as king; but he did not flee the reproach and the scorn when the Jews wanted to hang him on the cross.
He would not encircle his head with a golden crown, but with a crown of thorns, as was done at his Passion.
He who reigns eternally in heaven would not reign for a time in this life. This world is not our homeland, but our exile;
therefore we should not set our hope on this deceitful life, but should hasten with good merits to our homeland, for which we were created, that is, to the kingdom of heaven.
Truly it is written, "Whoever wishes to be a friend of this world will be counted God's enemy."
Christ said in a certain place that "The way that leads to the kingdom of heaven is very narrow and steep; and the way that leads to the torment of hell is very wide and smooth."
The way that leads to the kingdom of heaven is narrow and steep because we must earn our homeland with hardship.
If we wish to have him, we must love mercy, and chastity, and truth, and righteousness, and humility,
and have true love toward God and toward men, and give alms according to our means, and keep moderation in our food, and practise every other holy thing.
We cannot do these things without hardships; but if we do them, then with those labours, through God's help, we can climb the steep way that leads us to eternal life.
The way that leads to destruction is broad and smooth because sinful desires bring a man to destruction.
It is very easy for him, and no toil, to satisfy his lust, and to indulge in drunkenness, and greed, and pride, and to rob the weak, and to do whatever he pleases:
but these vices and others like them lead him without toil to eternal torments, unless before his end he ceases from evil and does good.
Foolish is the traveller who takes the smooth way that misleads him, and forsakes the steep one that brings him to the city.
So too we are truly foolish if we love brief ease and passing pleasures so much that they bring us to eternal torments.
So let us take the harder way, so that we toil here for a while, in order that we may be without toil for ever.

Christ could easily, if he had wanted, have lived in this life without hardships and gone to his eternal kingdom without suffering and without death; but he did not want to. About this the apostle Peter said,
"Christ suffered for us and gave us an example, so that we should follow in his footsteps"; that is, we must suffer something for the love of Christ and for our sins.
That man suffers well, and pleasingly to God, who fights against vices and does good as best he can.
He who is unwilling to suffer anything in this life will have to suffer worse sufferings against his will in the life to come.

Now a pure and holy season approaches, in which we must make amends for our negligence: therefore let every Christian come to his confessor, and confess his secret sins, and make amends according to his teacher's instruction;
and let each urge the other to good by good example, so that all the people may say of us, as was said of the blind man when his eyes were enlightened;
that is, All the people who saw that miracle praised God, who lives and reigns for ever without end. Amen.
